title: Fifty-two letters
hook: Guru Arjan's long acrostic on the letters, a school for the soul (Gauri, ang 250)

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Guru Ram Das: a routine, a city, and songs of longing. Your line was the fourth guru's way. What did you set out for this morning, and was it there when you woke? Day one thousand two hundred.

A, apple. B, ball. C, cat. The alphabet chart on a classroom wall sticks a picture to each letter, and some of those pictures never quite come unstuck. Now take that same schoolroom trick and aim it somewhere else. Each letter opens a short lesson, not about apples or cats, but about the mind, the ego, death, grace, and the Name. That's what Guru Arjan, Guru Ram Das's son, did in a long hymn in Raga Gauri. It has a name that tells you what it is: Bavan Akhri. Today's word.
screen: `A, APPLE. B, BALL.` → `EACH LETTER, A LESSON.` → `GURU ARJAN, IN GAURI.`

segments.voice: The hymn's own title says it: Bavan Akhri, fifty-two letters. It's an acrostic: stanza after stanza begins on a letter, and the letter becomes the doorway into a teaching. You could call it a school for the soul, with the alphabet as its timetable. But before the first letter, there's a salok, and it tells you who the teacher is. Paraphrased: the Divine Guru is mother, the Divine Guru is father, the Divine Guru is master and the Transcendent Lord. The Guru is companion, the destroyer of ignorance, kin and brother. So this school doesn't begin with a lesson. It begins with a relationship. The teacher is also a parent, a friend, the one who stays. Then the letters come. And here's where the carry comes in: the letters again. This path has been circling letters for a long time. In the first year we heard the story of young Nanak asking his village teacher what the letters really pointed to. We heard the tradition of Guru Angad shaping the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people could read the hymns. We heard Japji say that through letters, the Name is spoken and praise is sung. The Bavan Akhri stands in that line. Letters, for the Gurus, aren't only for contracts and shopping lists. They're a way to the Name, if you learn them for what they point to. That's the quiet point of an acrostic. Letter after letter gets its turn, and each one is taught to point the same way. Tomorrow we'll hear one of those letters speak.
screen: `BAVAN AKHRI: FIFTY-TWO LETTERS.` · `FIRST, THE TEACHER: MOTHER, FATHER.` · `THE LETTERS AGAIN, ON THIS PATH.` · `THE WHOLE ALPHABET POINTS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `A SCHOOL FOR THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a letter's lesson. Take the first letter of your own name. In the sit, let the breath slow and hold that letter in your mind, the way a child traces it on a slate. Then let it carry one lesson: a word that begins with it and is worth living by. Patience, if it's P. Kindness, if it's K. Don't search hard. Take the first good one that comes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bavan Akhri. Fifty-two letters: Guru Arjan's acrostic in Raga Gauri, where each letter opens a lesson and the Guru is the teacher. Today's word.
Your line: the letters again. Each time you write your name today, let its first letter remind you of the lesson you gave it. Day one thousand two hundred.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and study the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and its opening salok, on the Guru as mother and father, is recited and sung in Sikh prayer and kirtan.
